segments.text: Hi everyone, thanks for being here. I'm
Matthew, the CTO of Agent Fabric, and
today I'm going to talk about what it
actually takes
to solve the four-legged identity
challenge, and specifically why security
and identity become defining problems
once you move beyond local deployment.
The framing I'm going to use here is
what we call the four-legged identity
challenge. But I want to clarify one
thing in the beginning. It's that four
legs is actually just the minimum viable
complexity. In real world systems, you
often end up using five, six or longer
delegations.
Complexity grows very quickly and
systems we're used to, especially oath
are not designed for that. So what I
want to do today is walk through how we
got here, why traditional models break,
and then how can we build models that
actually safe to deploy.
So let's start with how OOTH was
originally designed. You can see here
that we have a diagram of how
traditional OOTH works. We have three
actors. The user, the application, and
the identity provider. The user sends a
request to the identity pro uh to the
app which then sends a request to the
identity provider
which then requests that the user goes
through authentication.
Then the user grants consent to the app.
The application receives an access
token. This is a very clean system. The
token represents the user
and the app has access is delegated to
to do stuff on user's behalf. The
delegation is simple and explicit.
There's only one hop here. And we know
exactly who is acting. There's no
reasoning layer. So there's no switching
identities. And who holds a token is who
executes the request.
So now
let's add an API call to this model so
we can extend it by introducing a
downstream API. So what this does is it
takes the access token from the IDP then
calls the API. The API will validate the
token. It will check for any scopes and
enforce any authorization then proxy the
call. So this is still within the OOTH
confines that we have today because the
system is distributed across services
and the identity model is still intact.
The API sees the identity enforces
permissions.
Delegation chain is still short. So this
is what we call the three-legged flow.
App executes user intent through an API.
There's no autonomous system, no
decision-m layer and it's purely
deterministic. And this is the reason
why OOTH scaled so well. The entity
acting is the entity authorized which is
a core assumption that OOTH holds.
And now this is where things start to
change. So up until now applications
directly executed user actions with
agents that assumption breaks. We can
introduce two new components an agent
and an MCP server. The flow becomes user
to agent to MCP server then to API. And
this is where OSH starts to fail.
It's because the application is no
longer the final executor. It holds
control to an agent which then decides
what actions to take. The MCP server
then executes those decisions against
downstream APIs. What used to be a
single delegation is now multihop and is
dynamic because of the agent. This
creates a key ambiguity. When the API is
called, we have the question of whose
identity is being used, the user, the
agent or the MCP server. And ooth
doesn't handle this well. Tokens are
bound to an audience can't be reused and
in this model identity gets lost across
the chain across the chain. If MCP
server uses zone credentials, the API
sees only the server and not actually
the user. Thus, the result is what we
call identity lost midchain. It's the
core of the four-legged identity
challenge and leads to real world
issues.

four legs. As shown here, you can
introduce even more things. In this
chart right here, we see we added an
identity provider. The chain becomes
more complex. You you might be able to
add another agent calling another agent,
multiple MCP servers, or different IDPs
per service as seen here. Now, we see
that identity is not just being passed

how do we pass identity forward. it

across these very large graphical
systems over multiple hops and if
necessary across time that's where
traditional oath falls short.
So some patterns that I've seen people
use today are here on this slide. Um the
first is non-delegating client
credentials. What this means is that the
MCP server calls downstream APIs as

MCP's off, not the user off. Downstream

action. The second tok is token

that tokens are audience

challenge is that this token exchange or
it's an RFC protocol is not widely

next is pre-injected token. The
application fetches all tokens up front

IDP but it assumes you know all
downstream dependencies ahead of time

service. What this means is that

lot of customers would like to see.
